client: I've been really struggling lately with this new job I started at a tech startup a few months ago. It feels like no matter how hard I work, I'm always behind on something — there's always another deadline I'm missing or a project that's slipping. Honestly, I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, because the work is still going to be piling up whether I'm here or not.
therapist: It sounds like you're carrying a lot right now — and even the way you're speaking reflects that sense of urgency and pressure, like you're racing just to keep up. I hear some real discouragement in what you're sharing, including a feeling that even reaching out might not be worth it, and I want to gently challenge that thought — because the pile of work won't change, but the way you're relating to it and to yourself absolutely can. You took a step by being here, and that matters.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I guess that makes sense in theory, but I'm not sure how much "relating differently" to my workload is actually going to help when my manager is still going to expect those deliverables by Friday. It's like, even if I somehow feel better about the chaos, the chaos is still there waiting for me. I don't know, maybe I'm just being too practical about it, but it's hard to see how a mindset shift fixes a deadline.
therapist: You're being practical, not resistant — and that's actually worth honoring, because you're right that a mindset shift won't make Friday's deadline disappear. But I notice something in how you're speaking — there's a real tension there, like your mind is moving fast and working hard to stay on top of everything even in this conversation. What CBT would actually offer isn't a way to feel okay about chaos, but tools to help you think more clearly *within* it — like identifying which thoughts are adding pressure beyond what the deadline itself requires, so you're not fighting on two fronts at once.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: Okay, that actually lands a little differently — the idea of fighting on two fronts. Because honestly, I think part of what's exhausting me is not just the actual work but this constant voice in my head telling me I'm already failing, that everyone at the company can see I'm in over my head. But I'm not sure I even know how to separate those two things — like, where does the real pressure end and the extra stuff my brain is adding start?
therapist: That question — "where does the real pressure end and what my brain is adding begin?" — is actually the exact right place to start, and the fact that you're asking it tells me you're already beginning to separate them. Your voice carries that quality of someone thinking quickly, working hard to figure something out in real time, which makes sense given how much mental energy this inner critic is consuming alongside the actual work. A useful first step in CBT is to treat that voice — "everyone can see I'm failing" — as a hypothesis rather than a fact, and ask: what's the actual evidence for it, versus what your mind is predicting and catastrophizing?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: When I actually try to think about the evidence, I mean, nobody has explicitly told me I'm failing — my manager actually said I was "getting up to speed well" last week, which I kind of brushed off at the time. But here's the thing, treating it like a hypothesis feels almost too logical for how real that feeling is in the moment — like when I'm sitting at my desk at 11pm with three unread Slack messages, it doesn't feel like a thought I can just examine, it feels like the truth. I'm not sure I can pull off that kind of rational distance when I'm already in the thick of it.
therapist: What strikes me is that you just did something really important — you remembered your manager's feedback and noticed that you'd brushed it off, which is exactly the kind of evidence your inner critic doesn't want you to hold onto. And I hear you that at 11pm with Slack pinging, that rational distance can feel impossible — your voice right now has a kind of quiet intensity to it, like you're working hard to stay composed while sitting with something that genuinely weighs on you. So rather than trying to be a detached scientist in those moments, what if you built a small "pre-loaded" response — something you've already decided to remind yourself of, like your manager's exact words, so you're not trying to construct the argument from scratch when you're already overwhelmed?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I like the idea of having something already ready, but I'm a little worried that in that moment I'll just dismiss it the same way I dismissed what my manager said in real life — like my brain will just go "yeah but that was then, and right now everything is on fire." I guess my skepticism is that the inner critic feels pretty good at shooting down evidence when it wants to. How do you actually make the reminder stick when the anxiety is already running the show?
therapist: There's something quietly vulnerable in how you're raising this — like you're genuinely hoping this could work but bracing yourself for disappointment, and that combination deserves to be taken seriously rather than talked past. You're right that evidence alone often can't outshout anxiety in full swing, which is why in CBT we pair the reminder with something physical and grounding — a deliberate breath, stepping away from the screen for 60 seconds — because it interrupts the anxiety's momentum just enough to create a small crack where the reminder can actually land. The goal isn't to win an argument with your inner critic, but to slow the moment down just enough that you're not completely at its mercy.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: The "small crack" idea actually makes more sense to me than trying to logic my way out of it — I think I've been imagining it as this all-or-nothing thing where either the anxiety wins completely or I somehow defeat it, and that framing was making it feel hopeless. But I'll be honest, stepping away from the screen when I have three unread Slacks feels almost physically impossible, like there's this pull to just stay and deal with it or else things will get worse. I guess I'm worried that taking that 60 seconds will feel irresponsible rather than helpful.
therapist: The way you're speaking right now — softly, carefully, like you're weighing each word — tells me this isn't just an abstract worry, it's something that feels genuinely loaded for you, and I want to name that the belief "stepping away is irresponsible" is itself one of the thoughts worth examining. That pull to stay glued to the screen feels protective, but it's worth asking: in your experience, does staying and powering through at 11pm with anxiety running high actually produce better work, or does it mostly produce more anxiety? That 60 seconds isn't abandoning the problem — it's investing in your ability to actually handle it.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: Honestly, when I think about it, staying glued to the screen at 11pm usually just means I send a bunch of half-coherent messages and then lie awake replaying everything anyway — so no, it's not actually producing better work. But I think the irresponsibility feeling runs deeper than just the work itself, like if I step away it means I don't care enough, or I'm not the kind of person who takes things seriously. I'm not sure where that came from, but it feels pretty baked in.
therapist: There's something worth pausing on here — your words are reflective and almost matter-of-fact, but your voice is telling a different story, fast and loud and charged, like this just touched something that runs much deeper than work deadlines. You've actually made a really significant connection just now: that stepping away doesn't just feel inefficient, it feels like a verdict on your character — and that's a belief worth being curious about, because "I must stay engaged at all costs to prove I care" is an exhausting standard that no deadline actually requires of you. Where do you think that equation — rest equals not caring — first came from?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, very rapid speech

client: That question kind of stopped me, because my first instinct was to say "I don't know" and move on, but actually I think I do know — growing up, the people I respected most were always the ones who pushed through, who never complained, who were the last ones to leave. I think I absorbed this idea that exhaustion was proof of effort, and if you weren't running yourself ragged you probably weren't trying hard enough. It's uncomfortable to say out loud because it makes it sound like I've just been operating on this old script without ever questioning whether it actually makes sense.
therapist: The way you just said that — quickly, like you needed to get it out before you could second-guess yourself — tells me this recognition carries real weight, and I want to honor how significant it is to name a script you've been living by without ever choosing it. You're not broken or naive for having absorbed that message; you learned it from people you genuinely admired, and it made sense in that context — but you're now in a position, maybe for the first time, to ask whether exhaustion as proof of worth is a rule you actually want to keep following. That's not a small thing to see about yourself.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: It's strange because hearing you say "a rule you didn't choose" actually makes me feel a little less ashamed about it, like it wasn't some personal failing that I ended up here — but almost immediately I notice this other voice saying "okay but now that you see it, you have no excuse, so fix it." I think even my reaction to a moment of self-compassion gets turned into another performance standard. I guess what I'm sitting with is — how do you actually start letting go of a script that's been running for most of your life, when part of you still genuinely believes it's what's kept you going?
therapist: The way you just spoke — fast, high, like the words were tumbling out under pressure — and yet what you're describing is this incredibly tender moment of self-awareness immediately getting conscripted into another demand, and I want to name how exhausting it is that even compassion gets turned into a task. You've just identified something really profound: that the script is so deeply wired that it co-opts the very tools meant to loosen it, which means the answer isn't to *try harder* to let it go — that would just be the same pattern in new clothes. Letting go of a lifelong script starts not with fixing it but with moments exactly like this one, where you simply notice it running without immediately obeying it — and you're already doing that.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: That reframe — that noticing without obeying is already the thing — is somehow both a relief and a little disorienting, because I've spent so long equating progress with visible effort that "just noticing" feels too quiet, too small to count. I keep waiting to feel like I've done something, and you're kind of saying the doing is the noticing, which my brain is having trouble fully accepting. I think I believe you intellectually, but I'm not sure I trust it yet in my gut.
therapist: The way you're speaking right now — fast, high, like something in you is both reaching toward this idea and pulling back from it — perfectly mirrors what you're describing, and I think that tension *is* the work, not a sign that you're failing to grasp it. It makes complete sense that you don't trust it in your gut yet, because your gut has decades of evidence that quiet things don't count — one conversation isn't going to overwrite that, and it shouldn't have to. But notice that you're sitting with discomfort instead of immediately resolving it into action, and that right there is the muscle we're trying to build.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech
